output.title: The Cutting of the String
output.prologue: Come out on the cliff and mind the ice. Put your back to the cold and look up, the way your grandmother looked up before she sent you to bed. This is the walk the old women give the children in the dark months, from the pole down the Windward shore and out over the Leeward water. Each stop is a lamp, and each lamp has a hand in the story. Count them on your fingers. Do not let go of the rope.

stops.text: Begin at the pole, where the Drop Spindle turns and never sets. Mother Hesk sits there with her spindle, drawing the string out thin and winding it on the whorl so the islands will not drift. The string is tied to the islands like a line to a mooring post, and it holds. Then Aun came up the cliff with a knife in his belt. He was smiling. He only wanted to know how far the wind went.

Aun drew the knife across the string at the cliff edge, and the sky went up with a crack like a sail filling. The shore birds were left on the rocks with nothing to wind. Mother Hesk saw it from the pole. She did not shout. She kept count, as she does, of every bird that lost its line. Look at the star with the hooked end, still open like a beak at the wind.

Under both seas Orrun the Deep-Whale felt the islands jerk on his back, like a boat when the mooring parts. He has carried them since before the first net was knotted, and he did not know what had been cut. He rose to breathe, and his blow went up white through the cold. Now the sky catches that spray and holds it. Keep your eyes on the Whale's Blow, and do not blink.

When the sky drifted off, nobody could fly back to the islands to mend the nets. The nets were torn and wet on the poles, and the men had no way to reach them. Ennu the Kite-Wright sat up all winter with sailcloth in his lap and cod-bone in his teeth, sewing a hawk to watch the coast from above. The hawk hangs over the Windward shore still. Its job is to see the boats come home. It has never been thanked for it.

Out on the Upper Sea the boats lost their way in the dark. The men looked up for the harbour lamp and found only black, and those on the rocks could see nothing either. So Ennu sewed a lamp-kite from the last red sail and sent it up the cut string. Then Tavo the Gale came down the water laughing and tore it loose. The Lamp Kite still hangs there, small and stubborn, over the boats that are still out.

On the black rock under the Windward cliffs sits a shag who would not go in. One autumn Tavo the Gale came laughing over the rock and soaked her to the skin. She spread her wings to dry, and they were never dry, and she sat through the rain with them held out. Nobody could move her, not the sea, not the Gale. The old women say she keeps her wings out for the ones who went under and did not come home.

When the knife came down, the gulls were nearest the string and went first, flying up after the sky as though they could carry it home. One grey hen had a torn wing. She could not keep pace as the sky drifted, so she held on to the cut end in her beak and would not let go. She hangs over the Windward shore with her wings spread and her grip still tight. Gulls carry word between the islands and Vel. She never gave up the message.

Ennu carved a gull from whalebone the winter the boats stayed on the shingle. He gave it goat-hide wings and tied its string to Hesk's reel at the pole, so that word could still go up and come back. The gulls had gone off after the sky, and the boats had no one to carry their names. The bone gull goes up the string each morning with the count, and it has not yet come down wet.

Tamun's husband went out to haul the lines in a grey squall. Tavo the Gale came laughing over the Upper Sea and took his boat, and the man went aloft as a kite, with a sail of grey cloth that his wife had sewn. Now she flies the Widow's Shawl Sail alone, low over the water, on the calm days when the sea lies flat. The sea kept the man. It did not keep the cloth.

When old Tenu went aloft, his grandchildren sewed his name onto a strip of sailcloth, one knot for each letter. They flew it at midsummer, when the light stays up past the cliffs and the lines are easy to see. Names matter in the Ilvari sky. The sea took so many with no name left on any stern. So say the name aloud before the wind takes it, and count the knots with your fingers, the way Hesk does.

Aun wanted a second kite to fetch the first one back, and he was sure that was all it needed. Ennu the Kite-Wright cut the cloth from the best sail and the bone from the oldest goat, and warned him how the cane must bend. Aun worked until his hands were raw. Then he could not bring himself to fly it. Varuk hangs low in the Leeward sky, the kite Aun did not fly.

When Aun cut the string the sky went up so fast that Tavo came down the cold air to see what the noise was. He laughed, and the wind tore through the Leeward gulls and drove them south. One gull did not turn back. She went down past the last of the kelp, into water gone black and smooth, where the stars are thin. The old women say what is lost always goes south. Look low over the water for her.

When the string was cut, the drowned began going aloft by sea, and the sea would not give them back. They went up as lamps on the water, boats with no crews aboard. Kael the Netter casts for them every night off the Leeward edge, and every night the net comes up empty and wet. You can see the lamp-boat's line of stars beside him. He does not stop casting. Neither should you, when your own hands are cold.

A boat went out past the Leeward edge in the year the herring failed. Her name was painted on the stern in old red, and the sea took the paint before it took the boat. So she is the Nameless Lantern now. Children are told to say a name for her anyway, any name, and she takes it. The sky holds a great many boats that were never named aloud, and Kael still casts for them.

When Aun cut the string, the sky drifted off so fast that the boats of the Leeward Reach lost their way home. Hesk counted the missing from her pole, one by one, and she was not pleased. She does not forgive a lost boat, and she does not forget one either. So a tallow lamp was lit on every cliff to show the harbour, and this small light, burning low over the south, is that lamp still.

Hesk keeps count. At each new moon she calls the kite-makers to the cliff and asks them to fly the Tally Kite, and the wind counts the knots for her. Nothing is dropped. Every knot is one who came through the winter, or one who went aloft, and the count is never lost. The string was cut, but the count was not. So the children who learn to tie a knot are learning the count the sky will need when it comes home.
